title: Grand Theft Auto III: streaming Liberty City through 32 MB of memory
summary: DMA Design turned roads, sightlines and data placement into a streaming system that made a continuous 3D city possible on PlayStation 2.

sourceLabels.gta3-moma: Grand Theft Auto III in the collection

blocks.text: A city too large to load

Liberty City could not reside entirely in the PS2's 32 MB of main memory alongside vehicles, characters, audio and game logic. DMA Design divided the world into data that could be requested as the player moved. The goal was not to hold the city; it was to keep the immediate neighbourhood convincing while predicting what would be needed next.

Travel usually followed streets with readable bends, tunnels and bridges. Those routes gave the streamer time to retire distant sectors and fetch new geometry and textures. Islands and locked bridges also structured progression while limiting the earliest working set. Urban layout therefore served navigation, story pacing and storage mechanics simultaneously.
Traffic made reuse visible as variety

Cars and pedestrians were selected from limited pools, but colour, route and behaviour combinations produced movement that seemed larger than the raw assets. The engine adjusted density around memory and performance. A vehicle leaving view could release resources for something approaching, turning population into a managed stream rather than a permanent simulation of every citizen.

Radio stations, dialogue, effects and mission cues competed for disc bandwidth. Long music programs could be read predictably while geometry requests changed with the player's direction. Designers used transitions and brief pauses to mask heavier loads. The celebrated soundtrack depended on the same scheduling discipline as the streets outside the car.
Missions ran across a systemic map

Objectives reused the city rather than loading separate levels, so scripts had to coexist with traffic, police response and player improvisation. The engine created mission entities and protected important state while the general world continued around them. This mixture generated memorable accidents, but it also multiplied edge cases for testing.

Draw distance, fog, level of detail and occlusion controlled how much city the renderer exposed. These were not simply cosmetic compromises. They defined the time available to stream assets before the player could see them. A fast vehicle or unexpected turn tested the entire chain from disc layout to renderer.
A storage system became a genre template

Grand Theft Auto III's freedom is often described as a design breakthrough, but the design existed because streaming made continuity practical. Roads, missions, radio and population were built around a moving memory window. Later open worlds expanded the scale, yet the core bargain remains: predict where the player is going without making the prediction visible.
